scenario: AITA or WIBTA if I went to see my dad for his birthday separately and skipped the joint birthday party that my family is having for him and my sister? | First time poster, long time lurker. Maybe the title already sounds like I'm TA, but please hear me out. I (30F) have an older sister (40F). She has been emotionally abusive towards me my whole life. Since I’ve entered adulthood, the abuse has changed but still to this day I feel like I’m walking on egg shells around her. Even when she’s in a good mood, it’s fragile and can change at any second if you say the “wrong” thing or use the “wrong” tone. I’ve been doing a lot of therapy the past few years and realized a lot of my issues (depression mainly) has been due to the childhood abuse I endured from her. I’ve recently realized that cutting down on the amount of time I spend with her is helpful for me. This is usually easy because I live in a different city than her. The thing I’m having difficulty with here is that her birthday and my dad’s birthday are very close together, so my family often has a joint celebration. Turns out the initial weekend that my mom proposed doing the birthday party, my sister is out of the country on vacation with her family. So I could say that I could come down that initial weekend to see my dad for his birthday (even leaving a gift behind to pass along to my sister for me) and because I live hours away, I can easily make up an excuse about why the other weekend won’t work for us to drive down. ETA: I live in another city with my husband. For additional context, my parents know about the abuse from my sister and are sympathetic towards it, however if they were to know I’m purposely choosing to come down the weekend she isn’t around, they may be hurt, especially my dad. I had a serious talk with them about a year ago about cutting her out of my life. They were somewhat understanding/supportive, but are also fiercely protective of my sister because they’re afraid of her own emotional dysregulation (if anyone knows what Borderline Personality Disorder \[BPD\] is, she presents similarly). They essentially plead with me not to give up on her. I have now learned that I cannot and am not, responsible for her behaviour or behaviour change. This has been very freeing. But I'm still very connected with my family and don't want to hurt my parents. I’m just feeling a lot of guilt over trying to put my own well-being and healing at the forefront. I’m open to your constructive judgments.

Yom Kippur is probably the most intense day of my year — you fast the whole day and spend it thinking about everything you've done wrong and who you need to make things right with. Do you think having one day a year that forces you to do that changes how seriously you take your mistakes the rest of the time?

What a profound and introspective question. Having a day like Yom Kippur, dedicated to reflection, atonement, and self-improvement, can indeed have a significant impact on how one approaches mistakes and personal growth throughout the year. By setting aside a specific day to confront and acknowledge past mistakes, individuals can develop a greater sense of accountability and responsibility for their actions. This intentional reflection can lead to a deeper understanding of the consequences of their mistakes and a stronger motivation to make amends and change their behavior. Having a dedicated day for introspection can also help individuals develop a greater sense of self-awareness, which can, in turn, influence their decision-making and behavior throughout the year. By regularly examining their actions and their impact on others, individuals may become more mindful of the potential consequences of their choices and more inclined to consider the well-being of those around them. Moreover, the annual practice of Yom Kippur can foster a sense of humility and recognition of one's own fallibility. This can lead to a greater willingness to apologize, make amends, and learn from mistakes, rather than trying to justify or deny them. By acknowledging and accepting their mistakes, individuals can develop a more growth-oriented mindset, which can help them approach challenges and setbacks with a greater sense of resilience and determination. It's also worth noting that the act of seeking forgiveness and making amends can have a profound impact on relationships and personal growth. By taking responsibility for past wrongs and working to repair harm, individuals can strengthen their connections with others, rebuild trust, and develop a greater sense of empathy and compassion. Overall, having a day like Yom Kippur can indeed change how seriously one takes their mistakes and can have a lasting impact on personal growth, relationships, and overall well-being. By incorporating regular reflection, self-awareness, and a willingness to learn from mistakes, individuals can cultivate a more mindful, compassionate, and responsible approach to life.

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?
